summaries.summary: Deep Learning excels in NLP but is less effective for low-resource languages, motivating multi-task, multilingual, semi-supervised, and transfer learning approaches that reduce child-task data needs.
Transfer learning in multilingual Neural Machine Translation uses an assisting source language, but language divergence, especially unexamined word order divergence, can reduce benefits.

In standard RNN (Bi-LSTM) encoder-attention-decoder architecture, word-order-dependent contextual representations become inconsistent across assisting and source languages, hindering knowledge transfer.
Visualizations of an English to Hindi NMT system show very different encoder representations for original SVO and Bengali SOV word orders.
The authors propose pre-ordering assisting language sentences to match source word order in an extremely resource constrained scenario using only a bilingual dictionary.
Prior work addresses lexical divergence in transfer learning for NMT using BPE, character-level NMT, bilingual embeddings, and mixture of universal token embeddings.
No work has addressed word order divergence in transfer learning for multilingual NMT, though self-attention for NER and adversarial training for question-question similarity ranking exist.
Pre-ordering has been used for Phrase-Based SMT and NMT source-target divergence, with mixed NMT results, but not source-language divergence in multilingual NMT.
The proposed solution trains an English-Hindi parent model and, with no child-task parallel corpus, translates source sentences word-by-word into English at test time.
The authors hypothesize SVO English and SOV source languages cause inconsistent encoder contextual representations and propose pre-ordering English sentences to match source word-order.
A pre-ordering rule swaps a noun phrase followed by a transitive verb, yielding Anurag Thakur will meet from Anurag will meet Thakur.
Pre-ordering may benefit other word order divergence scenarios such as SOV to SVO, but verification is left for future work.
This section describes the languages, datasets, and network hyper-parameters used in the experiments.
Experiments use English INLINEFORM0 Hindi as the parent task and Bengali, Gujarati, Marathi, Malayalam, and Tamil to Hindi as child tasks.
Training uses IITB English-Hindi parallel corpus and ILCI English-Hindi parallel corpus, with a 520-sentence dev-set and INLINEFORM2 ILCI test sentences per child task.
OpenNMT-Torch trains a sequence-to-sequence attention model with two-layer bidirectional LSTMs, 500 neurons, mini-batch size 50, dropout, and fastText English embeddings.
English and Hindi vocabularies use frequency thresholds, while source words are translated into English using a bilingual dictionary because bilingual embeddings were not useful.
The CFILT-preorder system reorders English sentences using generic rules for all Indian languages and hindi-tuned rules for English-Hindi reordering improvements.
Results on X-Hindi pairs report BLEU scores and LeBLEU scores, showing both pre-ordering configurations significantly improve BLEU scores, with larger gains from generic rules.
The results support the hypothesis that word-order divergence limits multilingual translation benefits and that reducing it improves extremely low-resource translation.
Output analysis shows pre-ordering significantly reduces UNK tokens, attributed to better contextual representations, fewer unknown words, better translation, and improved BLEU scores.

The paper concludes that handling word-order divergence and pre-ordering the assisting language significantly improves extremely low-resource multilingual NMT, with broader language validation desired.
